overview: Coelophysis was a slender Late Triassic theropod, about two metres long, that inhabited the flood-plains of what is now the American Southwest around 215 million years ago. Its hollow limb bones kept it lightweight and fast; its narrow jaws bore small serrated teeth suited to catching lizards and small vertebrates.

The Ghost Ranch quarry in New Mexico preserves hundreds of Coelophysis individuals of all age classes in a single catastrophic deposit — one of the most productive Triassic sites in the world. These bonebeds allowed the first detailed study of growth and possible social behaviour in an early theropod.

articles.title: Discovery and the Ghost Ranch bonebed
articles.body: Named by Cope in 1889 from fragmentary material, Coelophysis became well known only after Colbert's 1947–48 Ghost Ranch excavations. Early claims of cannibalism — small bones in adult stomach regions — have been reinterpreted as belonging to small crocodylomorphs. A Coelophysis skull was carried to the International Space Station in 1998, the first dinosaur in orbit.

articles.title: Anatomy and locomotion
articles.body: Long lower-leg and metatarsal proportions indicate a fast runner. Two body morphs (gracile and robust) were once attributed to sexual dimorphism; this remains uncertain. The three-fingered hand bore curved claws and the S-shaped neck allowed rapid strikes at small prey.

articles.title: Ecological context
articles.body: Coelophysis lived in a semi-arid, seasonally wet landscape alongside rhynchosaurs, aetosaurs and early crocodylomorphs. It was a generalist predator, and the Ghost Ranch bonebeds — possibly formed by drought-related aggregation around a shrinking waterhole — preserve the most complete Triassic ontogenetic series known for any dinosaur.

record.description: Coelophysis bauri was a small early neotheropod from the Chinle Group of the south-western United States. The Ghost Ranch bonebeds contain hundreds of individuals and many articulated skeletons, making its anatomy and growth exceptionally well documented.
facts: The neotype AMNH 7224 stabilises C. bauri, and Rioarribasaurus colberti is an objective junior synonym.
A famous cannibalism claim was overturned when the supposed juvenile remains inside one ribcage were identified as a crocodylomorph.

presentation.heroLead: A slender Triassic predator preserved by the hundred at Ghost Ranch, giving one of the richest records of any early dinosaur.

animalParagraphs: Coelophysis was a lightly built, long-necked theropod of the Late Triassic, roughly three metres long but weighing only about the same as a large dog. It had a narrow snout with small, blade-like serrated teeth, long legs, a long stiffening tail and grasping three-fingered hands, and lived on the river floodplains recorded by the Chinle Group of the American south-west.

It was named in 1889 by Edward Drinker Cope from scrappy bones collected near Abiquiu, New Mexico. Its fame came in 1947 when an American Museum team led by Edwin Colbert opened a quarry at Ghost Ranch that yielded hundreds of skeletons, many complete and articulated, ranging from juveniles to adults. A skeleton from that quarry, AMNH 7224, was made the neotype in 1996 to fix the name.

The bonebed has fed speculation about herds and cannibalism. The mass burial is now read as animals killed and concentrated by floods rather than proof of social living, and the supposed juvenile Coelophysis inside two adults' ribcages proved to be small crocodile relatives. What is secure is the anatomy: Coelophysis is the reference point for early theropod skeletons.
animalHighlights: A slender skull with serrated teeth and a kinked upper jaw typical of coelophysoids.
Hollow, thin-walled bones gave the genus its name, "hollow form".
Hundreds of individuals from one quarry document growth from juvenile to adult and two adult body forms.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Serrated teeth and gut contents including small reptile bones show a diet of small animals; the earlier cannibalism claim was withdrawn.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs and a lightweight build in articulated skeletons indicate a fast two-legged runner; actual speeds are modelled, not measured.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Complete adult skeletons give reliable lengths; mass estimates of around 15 to 25 kilograms depend on the method.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions are secure; no skin, feathers or colour are preserved, so the external covering is reconstructed.

presentation.classificationSummary: Coelophysis is the name-bearing genus of Coelophysidae and Coelophysoidea, a group of slender early neotheropods. Because its skeleton is so well known it anchors most analyses of early theropod relationships. Several species and specimens once assigned to it, including material from Africa and Arizona, are now placed in other genera.

related.reason: A larger, crested Early Jurassic theropod from the same region, often compared as a later coelophysoid-grade form.
A larger European coelophysoid of similar age known from two partial skeletons.
A small Early Jurassic coelophysid from Arizona known from a single partial skeleton.

questions.title: Did it live in groups?
questions.copy: Hundreds of animals buried together suggest a gathering, but flood transport and a drought-stricken water hole can produce the same result. The bonebed is not proof of pack living.

questions.title: What are the two adult body forms?
questions.copy: Adults fall into robust and gracile morphs. Sexual dimorphism is the usual explanation, but individual variation has not been ruled out.

questions.title: How much of the old record belongs here?
questions.copy: Coelophysis-like bones from Arizona, Zimbabwe and elsewhere were once referred to the genus; most are now assigned to other taxa, leaving Ghost Ranch as the core sample.

review.ageReviewNote: Diagnostic C. bauri material is late Norian to Rhaetian in the Chinle Group, especially the Rock Point Formation.

panel.headline: Hundreds of skeletons from a single Triassic quarry.
panel.standfirst: Coelophysis bauri is among the best-represented early dinosaurs, with hundreds of individuals, many complete and articulated, from the Ghost Ranch quarry in New Mexico. Its anatomy and growth are known in a detail few Triassic animals approach.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented by multiple articulated individuals across a growth series, from juveniles to two adult morphs.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls with teeth, full vertebral columns and tails, furculae, shoulder and hip girdles, forelimbs with hands and hindlimbs with feet, in many articulated skeletons, plus gut contents in a few individuals.
knownRemains.note: Nearly all of this material comes from one quarry, so the sample records one population and one moment; earlier referred material from elsewhere is now largely reassigned.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete skulls with dentition, braincases and hyoids, at several growth stages.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ribs, gastralia and chevrons in articulated skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Furculae, complete pectoral and pelvic girdles, forelimbs with three-fingered hands and a reduced fourth digit, hindlimbs and feet.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Gut contents preserved in a few skeletons; bone histology across the growth series. No skin, feathers or colour are known.

specimenCards.title: AMNH 7224 · neotype
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete articulated skeleton excavated at Ghost Ranch in 1947. Because Cope's 1889 syntypes were fragmentary and undiagnostic, the ICZN designated this specimen as neotype in 1996, making Rioarribasaurus an objective synonym.
specimenCards.meta: Ghost Ranch, New Mexico · Rock Point Formation · American Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: Ghost Ranch blocks
specimenCards.description: Large blocks of overlapping skeletons quarried between 1947 and the 1980s and distributed to museums across North America. They include juveniles, robust and gracile adults, and the individuals once thought to show cannibalism.
specimenCards.meta: One bonebed · hundreds of individuals · flood-accumulated

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Hundreds of skeletons of one species from one quarry, with complete skulls, limbs, tails and gut contents, spanning juveniles to adults.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A fast, bipedal predator of small animals; the mass burial reflects flood concentration, and the two adult morphs are usually read as sexes.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether it lived in groups, the cause of the two adult body forms, the external body covering and colour, and which Coelophysis-like fossils elsewhere truly belong to the genus.
